clue.text: How to follow the teams for entertainment

indicators.note: the word how comes after the teams, so it is placed second in the answer

parts.note: the two teams in a game are the sides
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks how they can keep up with the teams for a bit of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' puts HOW after SIDES. 'How to follow the teams' reads as a request for advice about watching sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground booth or minor attraction beside the main event is a lesser form of entertainment.

clue.text: Royalist unhappy, like. Wordsworth's reaper

indicators.note: an unhappy arrangement is a disturbed one, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gloomy Cavalier is compared to the figure in a famous Wordsworth poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhappy' rearranges the eight letters of ROYALIST. Wordsworth's poem 'The Solitary Reaper' describes a lone Highland girl singing as she cuts grain.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's reaper works alone in the field, the lonely figure of his poem's title.

clue.text: He is' expected to provide the correct solution

definitions.text: He is' expected to provide the correct solution

parts.words: He is' expected to provide the correct solution
parts.note: reads like a puzzle-setter, but the solution is a liquid medicine made up by a chemist

explanation.surface: Someone is expected to come up with the right answer to a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacist who makes up prescriptions hands out the correct medicinal liquid.

clue.text: Flag carried into battle by a Moor

definitions.text: carried into battle by a Moor

explanation.surface: A banner is borne into a fight by a North African warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag' is not a banner but the iris-like marsh plant. Put this word with 'Moor' and you get Sedgemoor, the 1685 battle in Somerset, England, where Monmouth's rebellion was crushed.
explanation.definitionFit: Flag is a name for wetland plants such as iris, close kin to the grassy marsh plant; with 'moor' attached it names the battle of Sedgemoor.

clue.text: Players showing two pairs of 19 ?

parts.note: 19 across is a word for pairs, so two pairs of pairs make eight, the size of this group of musicians

explanation.surface: Card players lay down two pairs of a certain number.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 across is BRACES: a brace is two, so two braces of braces is eight performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of eight musicians is the ensemble formed by four couples.

clue.text: A key to start with

explanation.surface: Someone is handed a key to begin with.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin or bottle device is a kind of key for getting in, and the first item or batsman in a sequence is what comes first.

clue.text: They have a lot to be unhappy about, said Gilbert

definitions.text: They have a lot to be unhappy about, said Gilbert

parts.words: They have a lot to be unhappy about, said Gilbert
parts.note: recalls the song in The Pirates of Penzance about a constable's lot not being a happy one

explanation.surface: W. S. Gilbert remarks that certain people have much to complain of.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance the sergeant sings that 'a policeman's lot is not a happy one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert's lyric says the life of a constable is not a happy one.

clue.text: No Sandhurst girl

parts.note: taken as written
Sandhurst is the Royal Military Academy, abbreviated RMA

explanation.surface: A girl is refused entry to Britain's army officer college.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandhurst, in Berkshire, England, trains British Army officers; its old name was the Royal Military Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is a woman's first name.

clue.text: Hold out against one direction among the others

indicators.note: one piece set among the others means it goes inside them

parts.note: the rest means the others
S is south, a compass direction
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone stands firm against a single course while everyone else goes another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts S and I inside REST, giving RE-SI-ST.
explanation.definitionFit: To withstand or oppose something is to hold out against it.

clue.text: Can be raised East of Suez, according to Kipling

definitions.text: Can be raised East of Suez, according to Kipling

parts.words: Can be raised East of Suez, according to Kipling
parts.note: recalls Kipling's Mandalay, where east of Suez a man can raise something wanting a drink

explanation.surface: Kipling says something may be lifted up beyond Suez.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's poem 'Mandalay' the soldier longs to go 'somewhere east of Suez... where a man can raise a thirst'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's line has a man working up a craving for drink in the East.

clue.text: The die-hard's entrenchment

parts.note: the final trench where a stubborn defender makes a stand

explanation.surface: The fortifications of someone who refuses to give up.
explanation.definitionFit: A final desperate effort is named after the last trench a defender holds to the death.

clue.text: God of war follows many others

indicators.note: the god of war comes after many, so it is placed second

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword sign for many
Ares is the Greek god of war

explanation.surface: The war god comes after a crowd of other deities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'follows' puts ARES after L. The Lares were Roman household gods, other gods than Ares.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman household spirits are further deities beside the war god just named.

clue.text: The first person as object, or subject

parts.note: taken as written
me is the objective case of the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on whether the pronoun is object or subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammar terms 'object' and 'subject' set up a lesson on pronouns, but 'subject' means a topic.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the topic of a talk or essay.

clue.text: Rats count perhaps as such

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of the two words before could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Deserters are counted as rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges RATSCOUNT. The whole clue also defines: a rat is slang for someone who deserts their side.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats who desert a cause are people who change sides.

clue.text: What's left ? Right !

parts.note: a question about what remains, answered with a word that sounds like a contradiction

explanation.surface: Someone asks which way is left and is told right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' and 'Right' tempt a directions reading; 'left' means remaining, and 'Right!' is just agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: What remains after the rest has gone is the leftover matter.

clue.text: These vessels should not be kept out of port

definitions.text: These vessels should not be kept out of port

parts.words: These vessels should not be kept out of port
parts.note: reads as ships kept from harbour, but the port is the fortified wine

explanation.surface: Ships ought not to be kept from returning to harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessels' and 'port' suggest shipping; these glass vessels hold port wine, poured to separate the sediment.
explanation.definitionFit: Glass carafes for serving wine are vessels that ought to be kept filled with port.

clue.text: Mother completely surrounded by fruit?

indicators.note: the mother is surrounded, so she goes inside the word for completely

parts.note: in toto is Latin for completely, giving toto
ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: A mother is entirely hemmed in by fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded by' puts MA inside TOTO. The question mark admits the tomato is botanically a fruit though eaten as a vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: The red salad item is botanically a berry, hence fruit with a question mark.

clue.text: Men are, chiefly ruled, by this system

definitions.text: Men are, chiefly ruled, by this system

parts.words: Men are, chiefly ruled, by this system
parts.note: chiefly is read as by chiefs, the rule of a clan's headmen

explanation.surface: A remark that men are mostly governed by some system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chiefly' looks like 'mainly' but means 'by chiefs', the leaders of clans.
explanation.definitionFit: Organisation into clans led by headmen is the social order of a tribe.

clue.text: A painter of note

parts.note: a famous painter, and also someone who produces musical notes by blowing

explanation.surface: A distinguished artist.
explanation.walkthrough: James McNeill Whistler was an American painter famous for 'Whistler's Mother'; a whistler also makes notes.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter James McNeill Whistler shares his surname with someone producing tunes through pursed lips.

clue.text: They are naturally sold in pairs

definitions.text: They are naturally sold in pairs

parts.words: They are naturally sold in pairs
parts.note: game birds are sold in couples, and the trouser supports come as a pair of straps

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper's remark about goods that come two at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: A brace means a pair (of pheasants, say), and trouser braces are sold as a pair; 'naturally' because the word itself means two.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a couple of shot birds, so these are what pairs are naturally called.

clue.text: Posters need them, for sticking on

definitions.text: Posters need them, for sticking on

parts.words: Posters need them, for sticking on
parts.note: posters are people posting letters, who need something to stick on the envelope

explanation.surface: Bill posters need something to fix their notices to walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posters' suggests printed notices; here they are people who post letters and need postage to stick on.
explanation.definitionFit: People sending letters must attach postage labels to the envelope.

clue.text: In Perth perhaps, yet in England

indicators.note: perhaps signals the words before can be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Something might be found in the Scottish city of Perth, yet also in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges INPERTH. Perth is a Scottish city; Penrith is a market town in Cumbria, north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Penrith is a town in Cumbria, so it lies in England.

clue.text: Very poor, support for his show at the' seaside.?.

definitions.text: Very poor, support for his show at the' seaside

parts.note: the seaside entertainer performs on a pier, which holds up his show
rot is rubbish, something very poor

explanation.surface: A seaside performer's show is propped up on a feeble platform.
explanation.walkthrough: Seaside pierrot troupes, white-faced clowns in loose costumes, played on piers in English resorts. The whole clue describes him as well as building him.
explanation.definitionFit: The white-faced clown of seaside concert parties performed on a pier.

clue.text: As impetuous as a' hatter with part of his stock.

parts.note: from the saying mad as a hatter
a cap is one of the items a hatter sells

explanation.surface: A rash hat-maker with some of his goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'mad as a hatter' supplies MAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A madcap person acts on reckless impulse.

clue.text: One of Wimbledon's ins and outs

definitions.text: One of Wimbledon's ins and outs

parts.words: One of Wimbledon's ins and outs
parts.note: in tennis scoring after deuce the server's lead is called in, the receiver's out

explanation.surface: One of the details of how the tennis championships work.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London tennis tournament. After deuce the umpire calls 'advantage in' or 'advantage out'.
explanation.definitionFit: The point after deuce is the edge called in or out in tennis scoring.

clue.text: Flower that can be plucked by hand

definitions.text: Flower that can be plucked by hand

parts.words: Flower that can be plucked by hand
parts.note: a bloom picked by hand, or a stringed instrument plucked pizzicato

explanation.surface: A bloom easy enough to pick with your fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant name is shared with the stringed instrument, whose strings can be plucked.
explanation.definitionFit: The violet family's garden bloom shares its name with the alto string instrument whose strings are plucked.

clue.text: Transactions in the timber trade?

parts.note: business transactions, and planks of pine or fir sold as softwood

explanation.surface: Business done among wood merchants.
explanation.walkthrough: A deal is a business transaction and also a sawn plank of pine or fir.
explanation.definitionFit: Bargains struck are business agreements, and planks of fir are softwood boards.

clue.text: He doesn't know why he's been capped

explanation.surface: Someone ignorant of why he has been selected for his country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capped' suggests an international sports cap; here it is the pointed paper hat once put on a slow pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow pupil is an ignorant one, and was made to wear the conical paper hat in class.

clue.text: Sugarloaf shape is about right for the old woman

indicators.note: the shape is about the letter, so it goes round it

parts.note: a sugarloaf is a cone of hard sugar

explanation.surface: A sugar-cone shape suits an old lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is about' puts R inside CONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A crone is a withered elderly woman.

clue.text: One of those blooming long-livers ?

parts.note: blooming sounds like a mild oath, but it means flowering plants that last for years

explanation.surface: An exasperated remark about one of those people who live forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blooming' reads as a British mild expletive; it means flowering, of a plant living several years.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that flowers year after year lives a long time.

clue.text: This worthy is commendable

parts.note: the word before worthy forms a compound meaning deserving commendation

explanation.surface: A notable person is said to be admirable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worthy' looks like a noun, a notable person; it is the end of a compound adjective, which is the 'commendable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to worthy, this word for acclaim makes an adjective meaning deserving commendation.

clue.text: A heavy cold when getting a flying decoration ?

definitions.text: A heavy cold when getting a flying decoration

parts.words: A heavy cold when getting a flying decoration
parts.note: someone with a heavy cold has a running nose, and a party ribbon flies in the air

explanation.surface: Someone picks up a bad cold just as they receive an air-force medal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying decoration' suggests an RAF medal; it is a paper ribbon, and a heavy cold leaves eyes and nose running.
explanation.definitionFit: A long ribbon of coloured paper flutters at parties, and a sufferer with running eyes is one too.
